title: Professional judgement and influences on decisions
blurb: Explain the reasoning behind your decisions, spot personal and external influences, and keep professional boundaries.
question: A midwife strongly believes every woman should breastfeed. A woman who has made an informed decision to formula feed asks for help making up bottles. What should guide the midwife's response?

teach.body: SPM 1.18 asks midwives to explain the rationale behind their own judgements and decisions, and to recognise and address any personal and external factors that may unduly influence them, in routine, complex and challenging situations. Formally, professional judgement is reasoning from evidence, assessment and the woman's preferences. In plain English: you should always be able to say why you did something, and be honest with yourself about what else might be pushing you.
teach.cite: NMC Standards of proficiency for midwives (2019) 1.18, 1.14

teach.h: What a sound decision rests on
teach.caption: NICE guidance is not mandatory, but professionals must take it fully into account alongside the individual's needs and preferences.
Code 1.3: avoid making assumptions and recognise diversity and individual choice. Code 19.2: take account of human factors.

teach.body: In Montgomery, the obstetrician did not discuss shoulder dystocia because she felt that, if told, diabetic women would choose caesarean birth and that caesareans were not in the mother's interests. Lady Hale said this looked less like a purely medical judgement and more like a view that vaginal birth is somehow morally preferable. A woman is entitled to weigh her own values alongside the medical evaluation of the risks.
teach.cite: Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11 paras 114, 115

teach.h: Boundaries and beliefs in the Code
head: Code
Expectation
rows: Stay objective; clear boundaries, including past patients
Do not express personal beliefs inappropriately
Refuse all but the most trivial gifts
Conscientious objection: limited cases; arrange cover
Resolve differences of opinion by informed debate

teach.body: Chloe has made an informed decision to formula feed. Her midwife, Bea, feels strongly about breastfeeding. Bea recognises this as a personal value that must not shape her care (SPM 1.18; Code 20.7). She checks Chloe has the information she wanted, respects her decision, and teaches safe preparation: water at least 70 °C, boiled no more than 30 minutes earlier, water in the bottle before the powder. She records the advice given, not her opinion.

teach.h: External pressure: name it, escalate it
teach.body: When staffing or workload pressures start to affect care (for example a delay of more than 30 minutes in giving pain relief, or a midwife unable to give one-to-one care in established labour), these are midwifery red flags. The midwife in charge decides whether staffing is the cause and what action to take. Pressure is a reason to escalate, not a reason to lower the standard of care.
teach.cite: NICE NG4 Box 3 midwifery red flags

teach.text: Best interests (SPM 1.14) is not 'what I think is best'. For a woman with capacity, her informed decision stands, even when it differs from your advice or personal values. Your judgement shapes the information and care you give, not her choice.

items: SPM 1.18: explain the rationale for your decisions; recognise personal and external influences.
Sound judgement combines evidence, assessment and the woman's values; NICE guidance is taken fully into account, not applied blindly.
Montgomery: value judgements dressed up as medical advice deprive women of free choice.
Code 20.6, 20.7, 21.1: boundaries, no inappropriate personal beliefs, no non-trivial gifts.
Staffing pressure is escalated (NG4 red flags), never absorbed by cutting care.

summary: You can now explain the reasoning behind a midwifery decision and recognise the personal and external factors that might bias it. You can keep professional boundaries and respond to pressure by escalating rather than compromising care.

A.q: A midwife is asked by a colleague why she advised a woman to come to the unit. Which response best meets SPM 1.18?
options: 'It is my usual practice in that situation'
'Her history and findings met our guideline criteria'
'The coordinator told me to bring her in for review'
'I had a strong feeling something was not right'
A.why: SPM 1.18 asks midwives to explain the rationale for their judgements: linking findings and evidence to the decision.

whyNot.2: Following an instruction does not explain her own clinical reasoning.
whyNot.3: Professional concern matters, but it should be explained with what she observed.

A.q: A woman who gave birth six months ago sends her former midwife a friend request on social media. What should the midwife do?
options: Accept, as care has finished
Accept but avoid discussing her care
Decline and keep professional boundaries
Accept if the woman's partner agrees
A.why: Code 20.6: clear professional boundaries with people in your care, including those who have been in your care in the past. NMC guidance warns against using social networks to build relationships with patients.

whyNot.0: Boundaries extend to people previously in your care.
whyNot.1: Accepting still creates a personal relationship with a former patient.
whyNot.3: The partner's view is irrelevant to the midwife's boundaries.

A.q: A midwife with strong religious views is caring for a woman who has chosen termination for fetal anomaly. Which action is consistent with the Code?
options: Share her views so the woman can reconsider
Provide compassionate care without comment
Ask the woman to confirm she is sure
Give leaflets about adoption services
A.why: Code 20.7: do not express personal beliefs (political, religious or moral) to people in an inappropriate way. She provides compassionate, non-judgemental care.

whyNot.0: Sharing personal beliefs here is inappropriate and could cause distress.
whyNot.2: Questioning a decision already made, without clinical reason, reflects her views rather than the woman's needs.
whyNot.3: Offering adoption information unprompted imposes the midwife's values.

B.q: In established labour, a woman has waited 40 minutes for pain relief because the ward is short of midwives. What does this represent?
options: An expected delay on a busy ward
A midwifery staffing red flag
A matter for the woman's partner to raise
A delay to record but not act on
B.why: NICE NG4: a delay of more than 30 minutes in providing pain relief is a midwifery red flag; the midwife in charge decides whether staffing is the cause and what action to take.

whyNot.0: This delay meets a red flag; it is not an acceptable norm.
whyNot.3: Red flags require action, not just documentation.

B.q: A formula milk company offers to fund a midwife's conference place if she shares its leaflets with women. What should she do?
options: Accept, as CPD benefits women
Accept and declare the funding
Decline the offer
Accept if leaflets are evidence-based
B.why: Code 21.1: refuse all but the most trivial gifts, favours or hospitality. Accepting would create a conflict of interest and promote a commercial product to women; Baby Friendly standards also exclude promotion of breastmilk substitutes.

whyNot.0: Professional development does not justify promoting a commercial product.
whyNot.1: Declaring the funding does not remove the conflict of interest.
whyNot.3: The problem is the commercial arrangement, not the leaflet content.

B.q: After caring for a baby who died following shoulder dystocia, a midwife notices she now advises every woman with a large baby to have a caesarean. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Continue, as it is the safer option for women
Refer all such women to the consultant clinic
Stop discussing birth options with these women
Reflect on whether past events bias her advice
B.why: SPM 1.18 asks midwives to recognise personal factors (such as a distressing past case) that may unduly influence decisions. Reflection, ideally with supervision or support, comes first.

whyNot.0: Advice should reflect each woman's risks and preferences, not one past case.
whyNot.1: Referral may sometimes be right, but blanket referral is driven by the same bias.
whyNot.2: Women need balanced information to make choices (Montgomery).

C.q: A woman requests a caesarean birth because of severe anxiety about vaginal birth. Her midwife believes vaginal birth is better for women. Which response best reflects Montgomery?
options: Advise against a caesarean and reassure her
Discuss her reasons, risks and benefits of both
Tell her caesareans are for medical reasons
Arrange a caesarean without further discussion
C.why: Montgomery paras 114 to 115: the woman is entitled to weigh her own values alongside the medical evaluation of risks. The midwife explores her reasons and gives balanced information, offering perinatal mental health support.

whyNot.0: This lets the midwife's preference shape the advice.
whyNot.2: This is inaccurate and shuts down the discussion.
whyNot.3: She is entitled to information and discussion, not just a booking.

C.q: A midwife asked to assist with a surgical termination says she has a conscientious objection. What must she do?
options: Leave the theatre and let the team cover her role
Assist this time and register her objection afterwards
Tell colleagues and arrange a colleague to take over
Explain her beliefs to the woman before leaving
C.why: Code 4.4: tell colleagues, your manager and the person receiving care, and arrange for a suitably qualified colleague to take over. Objection is limited (Abortion Act s4) and does not apply where treatment is needed to save life or prevent grave permanent injury.

whyNot.0: Leaving without arranging a qualified colleague to take over puts the woman's care at risk.
whyNot.1: She may object, but must follow the Code's process.
whyNot.3: She tells the woman she has an objection, but must not share personal beliefs inappropriately (20.7).

C.q: A midwife is under pressure to discharge a postnatal woman to free a bed. The woman's blood pressure is 152/101 mmHg and she has a headache. What should guide the midwife's decision?
options: The bed manager's request
The time since the birth
The woman's wish to go home
Her clinical assessment
C.why: SPM 1.18: recognise external pressures that may unduly influence decisions. A raised BP with headache needs medical review (pre-eclampsia can present postnatally); discharge depends on clinical findings.

whyNot.0: Bed pressure is an external factor that must not override clinical safety.
whyNot.1: Time since birth does not make her safe for discharge.
whyNot.2: Her wishes matter, but she needs information about her findings and review first.

reteach.title: The mirror test
reteach.question: Before you act, look in the mirror: what is really driving this decision?

blocks.body: Is this decision based on her assessment and the evidence? Is it what she wants, once informed? Is anything else pushing me: my beliefs, my last difficult case, tiredness, the bed manager, a colleague's seniority? If the third answer is yes, name it, reflect, and if needed escalate or ask a colleague for a second view.

blocks.text: Pressure is not a rationale. 'We needed the bed' or 'I always do it this way' would not stand up as the reason for a clinical decision.

explain.body: SPM 1.18: explain the rationale behind judgements in routine, complex and challenging situations. A rationale links findings and evidence to the decision and to the woman's wishes.

test.q: Which statement is a professional rationale for a decision?
options: 'The woman seemed difficult and was not listening'
'Unit policy says women like her are referred'
'BP 150/100 on two readings meets referral criteria'
'The registrar was busy, so I made the decision'
test.why: A rationale links objective findings with evidence-based criteria.

whyNot.0: This is a judgemental impression, not a rationale.
whyNot.1: Policy may be relevant, but the rationale should explain how the findings meet it.
whyNot.3: Colleague availability is an external factor, not a rationale.

explain.body: Beliefs, values, previous experiences, fatigue and assumptions can bias advice. Code 1.3: avoid assumptions; 20.7: do not express personal beliefs inappropriately.

test.q: A midwife assumes a 17-year-old will not want to breastfeed and does not discuss it. Which Code standard is breached?
options: 1.3: avoid making assumptions
10.1: keep timely records
13.5: complete training first
21.1: refuse gifts
test.why: Code 1.3: avoid making assumptions and recognise diversity and individual choice.

whyNot.1: This is about records, not assumptions in care.
whyNot.2: This is about training before a new role.

explain.body: Staffing, bed pressures, targets, hierarchy and commercial interests. NG4 red flags: escalate to the midwife in charge. Conflicts of interest (including financial) are declared and avoided.

test.q: A midwife cannot give one-to-one care to a woman in established labour because she has two women. What should happen?
options: Report it as a staffing red flag
Continue and document the pressure
Ask the partner to monitor contractions
Move one woman to the postnatal ward
test.why: NICE NG4: any occasion when one midwife cannot provide continuous one-to-one care in established labour is a red flag; the midwife in charge decides on action.

whyNot.1: Documenting without escalating leaves the risk unaddressed.
whyNot.3: Moving a labouring woman inappropriately is unsafe.

explain.body: Code 20.6: stay objective with clear boundaries, including with past patients and families. 21.1: gifts. 20.10: social media.

test.q: A woman's husband asks a midwife out for a drink after she discharges the family from her caseload. What should she do?
options: Accept, as care has ended
Accept if the woman agrees
Accept after six weeks
Decline and maintain boundaries
test.why: Code 20.6: clear professional boundaries with people in your care, including past patients, their families and carers.

whyNot.0: Boundaries extend beyond the end of care.
whyNot.1: The woman's agreement does not change the midwife's professional boundaries.
whyNot.2: No waiting period makes this appropriate.
